speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT OF 1944 EXTENDING ITS OPERATION FOR THREE Y EARS
speechtext:
Perhaps I might say a word at this point. The main purpose of the bill which will be founded on this resolution is to extend the present Farm Improvement Loans Act for a further period of three years, on the same basis as the present act. It expires on the last day of this month, and unless extended it would not be possible to extend further credits under it,
I am informed the act has worked out pretty well, and it is proposed to extend it for a further period of three years, with guarantees to the banks who make these loans on the same basis as they are now.
There will be an additional provision extending the type of security which may be taken, by enabling banks to take a mortgage or hypothec on the construction, repair, alteration or making of additions to any building or structure on a farm. Heretofore a bank could take this type of security only where the principal amount of a loan exceeded $2,000 and w'as for a period extending beyond five years. The security provided for loans under $2,000 for a period of less than five years is farm implement security. The proposed amendment is to make these loans available to farmers who are not in a position to give farm implement security. For example, there are certain types of farming where the farmer actually has no implements of any value upon w'hich to give security. In these cases he has not been able to get a farm improve-

Foreign Exchange Conservation
ment loan. There are other eases in which the only implements a farmer has to give security on are exempt, and this type of farmer finds himself unable to obtain a farm improvement loan. The proposed amendment is to take care of cases of that type.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext:
In the light of the discussion of schedule III on Friday evening it looks to me as though time could be saved if I made a statement covering the general principles of schedule III, giving the back-

ground of the administration of this schedule and discussing the moving picture and automobile items which seem to give so much distress to hon. members opposite.
The discussion which started on Friday on schedule III, dealing with the import restrictions to be applied to capital goods, revealed some basic misconceptions as to the purposes and form of the control. Before proceeding in detail I would like to make a short general introductory statement.
First, a word on the principles and policy underlying the administration of schedule III. It can be put very simply. The objective guiding our administration is to encourage industries, activities and practices -which will earn or save United States dollars. A necessary test is that these industries will use Canadian resources in so far as possible. New industries must be economically sound; capable of standing on their own feet and competing successfully once the temporary protection of import restrictions is withdrawn. That is the positive side.
To make our positive measures effective we must also apply some negative and restrictive measures. We must discourage further investment in a broad range of industries which are less essential. I do not like the word "nonessential." The new amusement, service, commercial and industrial enterprises in which new investment and construction must be curtailed would provide many pleasant amenities and improvements in the Canadian standard of living. But they all involve expenditures of United States dollars. I have mentioned before that approximately 30 cents out of every dollar spent on new construction, machinery and equipment finds its way to the United States. Since our supply of United States dollars is limited it must, in effect, be rationed.
The need for this is underlined by the magnitude of new capital investment intentions in 1948. On top of an investment boom in 1947 in which the all-time record, in peace or war, of $2-4 billion was spent on new construction, machinery and equipment in Canada, an increase of 17 per cent, or $400 million, is planned for 1948. For the purposes of this discussion it is the United States dollar aspect of this really staggering amount-$2-8 billiom-which concerns us. But I would like in passing also to draw attention to the disturbing inflationary possibilities inherent in such a program. Some postponement of the less essential expenditures in this program will be far from harmful. It will not cause any unemployment in the construction or capital goods industries. In fact our capacity in a

Foreign Exchange Conservation
number of key instances, such as steel supply, will be strained to the limit to provide for essential construction. Additional demand in the market will simply bid up prices, intensify shortages, interrupt necessary work and generally add to costs. On the other hand, projects postponed now will prove useful in maintaining employment and income in the future.
This may appear a digression, but I wish to make the point that while our exchange position forces us to limit our purchases of capital goods in the United States, our over-all investment picture is such that some deferment of expenditures would in any case be economically desirable and sound.
There are two possible methods of limiting the imports of capital goods, or to put it another way, of rationing our limited supply of United States dollars to be spent on such goods. One method is an over-all blanket reduction; the other is by a selective approach, distinguishing between those projects which are most necessary and helpful to Canada, and those which can be postponed with a minimum of loss and inconvenience.
There can be little question as to the superior merit of the second method-the selective approach. But it has some important implications, from its very nature, that must be clearly understood. It is obvious that no hard and fast formula can be laid down to govern administrative procedure. Almost every project has distinctive features which require special consideration. There must obviously be a measure of administrative discretion. Each application for an import is screened in the light of the use for which it is required. Wherever possible the importer is required to submit complete details of his project. Various factors must be taken into account in the final appraisal of the essentiality of the project such as, for example, the need for maintaining basic public services; the possibilities of expanding export trade, the desirability of further developing our primary industries and in general of strengthening the Canadian economy with an eye to maintaining employment and income in the future.
What I have been saying applies to the general range of capital goods covered by schedule III. The schedule also provides for control of the imports of the important automobile and motion picture industries. Since there has already been some desultory discussion of this I would like to make some general remarks concerning these two industries and their place in our over-all exchange and industrial program.
The automobile industry has become one of the largest Canadian manufacturing industries. It has developed to the point where cities such as Oshawa and Windsor are largely dependent upon it as a source of income and employment, and its ramifications are very great. Tire total scope of the industry cannot indeed be estimated with any accuracy because it extends into so many aspects of our national life. It reaches out from the automobile production line to distributors, repair and dealer services which extend across the country. The needs of automobile drivers and of commercial transport are reflected in the highway systems and the construction programs of the provinces. The tourist industry is important to the country because of the automobile and the service facilities available to travellers. The automobile manufacturers depend in their turn upon other industries which supply them with their raw materials, such as primary iron and steel, textile fabrics, plate glass, paints and varnishes, and so forth.
I have been asked to provide some statement as to what was our preliminary objective with regard to the saving of United States dollars which might be effected by restricting the imports of the automobile industry. I must say again that there was no such objective at the beginning except the general belief, founded on a careful examination of the facts, that some substantial saving could be made without at the same time inflicting damage on the industry itself. I have given the house a figure of $35,000,000 which was mentioned at an earlier stage by some of those involved but this was never a goal or an objective.
It has been necessary to proceed step by step in consultation with the industry itself. They have been approached to give their advice as responsible citizens in the formulation of a policy for their industry which would be in the national interest. A formula has been developed which will enable automobile manufacturing to continue at substantial levels and still provide some relief by way of minimizing the net drain of United States dollars.
The formula has been published and made available to the house and it will not require any marked diminution of automobile production in Canada this year. In the categories affected, namely automobiles and light trucks, it might indeed be increased from the high level of last year when the total production of such vehicles was in excess of 250,000. Imports of parts under tariff items enumerated in schedule III, namely 438b, 438c, 438d and 438e, amounted to $108 millions in 1947. Imports of complete vehicles, such as automobiles and trucks of three tons or less, were
Foreign Exchange Conservation

running at the annual rate of about $65 million! in 1947 unfil they were banned on November 17. Out of this total it is estimated that the formula will save about $70 to $75 millions of imports from the United States. By far the larger part of this, about $55 millions, will be saved1 on the import of complete vehicles and the balance on non-essential accessories and gadgets. Many parts which were previously imported will be found obtainable in Canada of good quality and at favourable price.
In effect the formula adopted reduces the imports of finished cars to token amounts in 1948, but will permit the continued operation of the automobile production and service industries at substantially 1947 levels. There is, in addition, an exchange incentive to increase production and exports above 99 per cent of the 1947 level, and1 the effect of this is that, roughly speaking, for every additional car sold for export two additional cars can be made.
Let me repeat that the formula and these estimates have been arrived at after consultation with the industry itself. I have 'been impressed by the way in which the industry has taken a responsible attitude towards this urgent national problem and has co-operated fully.
I should like to turn now to the motion picture industry. It illustrates that every industry has some special characteristics requiring special consideration. One approach to saving United States dollars in the motion picture business would have been to apply quotas to imports of United States films. This method has been applied in a number of other countries, but with results far from generally satisfactory. In addition, there are some special features in the case of Canada which make a simple quota basis of restriction inappropriate. A substantial amount of the United States dollar cost of the industry to us is in the earnings of United States motion picture properties in Canada. This is over and above the approximate $12,000,000 a year paid in rentals on imported films. The total annual exchange cost of the industry is estimated at $20,000,000, of which $17,000,000 is in United States dollars, the balance going to the United Kingdom and, to a smaller degree, to France. The financial facts of the movie industry in Canada, the tastes and habits of the Canadian movie-going public, and the harmonious relations we have enjoyed with the United States producers-in short, the special situation of the industry in Canada- called for a more imaginative and constructive approach than quota restrictions.
rvfr. Howe.]
As I mentioned' on Friday, discussions with the industry are proceeding. I do not think it would be desirable to go into detail on these while they are still under way. But I would like to say that we have been very much pleased with the co-operative spirit in which the industry has joined with us to explore the problem.
That Canada has some interesting possibilities in the movie world is obvious. Climatic factors, local colour and cultures, magnificent natural scenery, availability of technical personnel and facilities, and proximity to the California and New York centres of the United States industry are all of significance. The west coast and Quebec, to mention only two areas, have important location and production advantages. It is our hope that the movie industry will contribute to the solution of the Canadian exchange problem, not by contraction of business in Canada, but by the development of production in Canada and the use of the United States and international network of distribution outlets of the chief United States companies. An important by-product, of course, would be the publicity and resulting tourist business stimulated by a development of this nature.

speechtext:
My criticism of the minister's statement is that there is no permanency in his policy. In. the maritime 5849-96i
provinces we have a great natural building stone industry. It developed to a large extent years and years ago. Stone was produced in many parts of the maritime provinces and shipped not only to Ottawa and central Canada but also by vessel to a much larger extent to the United States. Many of the large buildings in New York, Boston and Providence were built out of stone produced in my constituency. It was produced not only in Cumberland county but also in the neighbouring counties of Westmorland and Pictou. The Langevin building in this city is built of stone produced in Northumberland county. Gloucester, Saint John, and Queens counties in New Brunswick also have stone quarries. In fact the geological formation of the maritime provinces is largely sandstone, and it is of a quality that cannot be surpassed anywhere. No better quality stone is produced anywhere than is produced in the quarries to which I refer. This parliament building is largely built of stone from Cumberland county. The old parliament building was built of Ohio sandstone. When it was destroyed by fire the architects unwisely used some of the old United States stone; they used it in the rear of this building, and it has disintegrated so that it is a blemish on this fine structure. If this building had been built entirely of stone from the maritime provinces there would not be the disfigured stones than can be seen in the rear of the building. The tower at the entrance is built of Cumberland county sandstone, and that is as fine an example of building material that can be found anywhere in the world.
This industry, like many others in the maritime provinces, has been retrogressing in recent years. A change has taken place in building methods. In the old days when our stone was shipped to the big centres, large strong blocks were used to support buildings of three, four, five and six stories. In recent years steel structures have been built with thin slabs of stone. Stone laying would perhaps be started on the second or third floor rather than at the bottom, the steel supporting the building rather than the stone as in the older days. The cement industry has advanced and artificial stone is produced which displaces part of the markets for stone, but there is no comparison in appearance or quality. The stone industry can be built up, and it would give a good deal of employment to the people in the maritime provinces. It would save Canadian dollars, which it has been necessary to save ever since I can remember-ever since the national policy was put into effect and before.

Foreign Exchange Conservation
Therefore my complaint is that there is no permanency to this policy of encouraging the use of Canadian products. W hen the Minister of Finance made his statement he said this policy was only temporary, and made an excuse for it because of that fact. If there were a permanent policy which gave some assurance and encouragement to the stone and building industry, scores of stone quarries would start up in the maritime provinces and would supply the stone requirements of all central and eastern Canada. But in the statement made to the house today by the minister there is no encouragement for these owners of stone properties to start operations. In the policy that has been in effect or is now before the committee there is no encouragement for the re-establishment of that industry; yet it was one of the most important industries in eastern Canada. The maritimes have not just one grade of stone; they have many grades, of different colours and textures. There is grey stone, blue stone, red stone-all the different shades.
My criticism of this legislation and of the statement made by the minister is that there is no permanency to the policy. The dominion government should adopt a policy-and I am glad that the Minister of Public Works is in his seat-of using in the construction of public buildings only such building materials as are produced in Canada. In Manitoba there are deposits of the stone which was used in the interior of this parliament building; it is a credit to Canada and a credit to Manitoba and should be used much more widely than it is. But architects and the government seem to give preference to the importation of United States stone. They can order any specifications and the big quarries in the United States are able to fill them more quickly than quarries in Canada can. because they have large plants whereas the industry in Canada has been allowed to lag for many years and now has only a fraction of the importance it held fifty or one hundred years ago.
In my province there was an old saying that if you put a grindstone or building stone in the waters of the bay of Fund}' or Northumberland strait it would float naturally to Boston or New York. That trade is a thing of the past, but we still have the deposits of stone. When the budget is brought down this policy should be put on a solid basis so that builders and quarrymen may be encouraged and the industry built up to the benefit of our economy. That is what this country wants and what the maritime provinces deserve.

I wish to support the stand taken by the hon. member for Cumberland. The complaint I have is this. There are three agencies using United States dollars to bring in stone, steel, and other expensive materials. First there is the agency which has to do with dominion buildings-customs houses, post offices and many other public buildings. The second group are the banks, many of whom are building skyscrapers with the housing situation as it is. When the Bank Act was up for revision three years ago I claimed that under the then section 92 they had no right to build these skyscrapers with practically all the stone imported from the United States. We should develop our own quarries throughout this country, as a national policy. They are in an experimental stage at the present time and have not been developed as they should be. The third group are the theatres, which are being built when we cannot get housing. Look at the housing situation in this city, where people are living in shacks and trailers in creeks and all that kind of thing.
These are the three groups who are carrying the large construction. The banks are the worst offenders. Under the Bank Act they have no right to go into real estate; their buildings must be commensurate with the size of their business. They cannot go into real estate except for collateral, and any shareholder has the right to bring an action against a bank under the act, or to go to treasury board and complain that the provisions of the act are not being lived up to. What is the position? The treasury board limits the banks to a period of seven years in which to get rid of these illegal properties, which require large quantities of expensive granite and other kinds of stone. That should be stopped. During the discussion of the Bank Act I asked the then Minister of Finance what he proposed to do in regard to the banks which were carrying on in this way, building thirty and thirty-five story skyscrapers as real estate investments, and he said an inquiry would be made into it. Under the act the treasury board can give a bank an extension of another seven years, making a total of fourteen years in which the bank must get rid of its real estate if the section is abused. If it does not do so the property reverts to the crown. But the Bank Act has not been carried out. Why should they go to work and use all this material, with
the housing situation as it is? Why should people be allowed to build expensive theatres? There is one west of the Maple Leaf Gardens. Another is being built on Bloor Street east of Avenue road, on the north side. It is a large building, using many materials which must be imported from the United States.
I support a policy of Canada for Canadians in connection with these three items. I believe we should utilize our own quarries and develop them further, using all the scientific discoveries that have been made in recent years. So I hope the minister will take these points into consideration, because this class of construction represents a large expenditure of United States dollars.

I have read five of these, but the sixth really gives an opportunity to the minister to show preference in favour of one at the expense of another. The sixth provides for the fabrication in Canada of a product or part formerly imported which is essential to Canada's economy. No. 6 gives the minster absolute power. It permits him to determine the economic development of this country in that he may allow one company to fabricate goods which were formerly imported and which are essential to Canada's economy. That is the one to which I make the strongest objection. No. 6 is an omnibus provision. If there are two or three individuals desiring to commence business in this country it places the minister in position to be able to say to one, "You can commence" and to say to the other, "You shall not commence."

I should like to ask the minister to elucidate upon and enlarge that point 6 which he placed before the Canadian Manufacturers Association. What are some of the industries which the minister believes could be set up in Canada to produce the products formerly imported which are essential to Canada's economy? Would the minister state two or three that are not operating today in this country but which could operate in producing goods essential to Canada's economy?

There are any number of parts industries which could operate here. Parts industries are expanding greatly, and the administration is encouraging their expansion. All that we ask of a new industry is that it make some real contribution to the Canadian economy. It is difficult to pick out of your mind any particular one. I might mention a company which has been set up to make shock absorbers for automobiles. All the shock absorbers which are made by this one manufacturer were formerly imported. That industry which has been set up to manufacture them in Canada falls into the category of an industry that is making a product essential to the Canadian economy.
Two million dollars are being spent in Hull in connection with an industry to make alcohol out of sulphite waste. There is a high United States content in that, but the resultant product will be a net gain to Canada and will represent either exports or a desirable domestic supply of industrial alcohol which is used in great volume. That is admitted as a desirable project.
There are several undesirable projects that run through my mind but I have not sufficient details before me to explain them. A new brewery would be an undesirable project, and we have turned down two or three applications. A new distillery would be in the same category, and new moving picture theatres and office buildings.

speechtext:
I am glad to hear the minister say that it is the policy of his department to induce industries to locate in Canada, and that this program will be, as desired by the hon. member for St. Paul's, a permanent policy. Has the minister or his officials made any effort to have industries established in the maritime provinces on a permanent basis for the good of the Canadian economy? It is recognized by everybody, including the minister, that the industrial policy adopted during the war was not fair to the maritime provinces. We did not share fairly in that. This is another opportunity when industry can be established in this country, and the minister indicates that it is being done in some places. My inquiry is whether any special efforts are being made by the minister or those engaged in working out this policy to induce industries to establish in the maritime provinces. Our misfortune is that our basic products and natural resources are largely shipped out of the province in the raw, unrefined form. From the county of my hon. friend the member for
Cape Breton South, for instance, enormous quantities of coal and a very large tonnage of iron and steel in the roughest form are shipped. Today's price of that steel is two and a half or three cents a pound. That steel could be manufactured in refining industries into products worth a thousand dollars and more a ton, and the same with coal. There are many different chemical industries based on the chemical ingredients of coal which could be established in our province. The leader of the C.C.F. party suggests gypsum to me. That is another raw material of which we have enormous deposits but which are now being shipped out largely in the roughest possible form. They could be refined in the province if industries were established there based on the requirements of Canada. That would give a measure of fairness to our province.
In the county of Cumberland a salt-refining industry has been started. We have fifty square miles of salt deposits, running from four to five thousand feet in thickness producing and refining 125 to 150 tons a day. But it is being shipped away as pure as any salt produced on the North American continent. This great natural resource could be the basis of many chemical industries which might be established in our province.
There is also the salt mine at Malagash.in the eastern part of Cumberland county. There we have a very large deposit, and the only salt-mining project in all Canada, shipped away in the roughest and cheapest form.
Our lumber is shipped away in the roughest possible state. It could be the basis of many industries if they were encouraged to establish there and had some assurance of permanency. The opportunity came during the war period to help balance industry in Canada by establishing industries with some permanency in the maritime provinces. Here is another opportunity now to establish permanent industries in the maritimes and do a measure of justice to that part of our country.
There has always been a shortage of United States currency in Canada. There has always been surplus of importations from the United States. We have always needed to conserve United States exchange. Why could industries such as I have mentioned not be established, based on the natural resources and production of the maritimes? I appeal to the minister to apply his attention and direct that of his officials to this field, so that industries can be encouraged to locate in the maritime provinces. The minister takes credit for having established industry in Central Canada; but,

But I am anxious to get information with regard to other items in schedule III. A good many of them cover structural steel. One item, 388b, covers steel which is not strictly structural. A good many other items cover various kinds of machines, traction machines, internal combustion engines, and so on. The minister, I think, is wanting to leave schedule III in general terms, telling us that he has not yet worked it out but that there are two methods, an over-all blanket reduction and the selective approach, and he feels that we should have the selective approach. I will get away from the minister's own terms, which apparently I did not understand. What I am referring to is a regulation such as we have for the motorcar industry whereby each manufacturer who imports shall be entitled to have so-and-so. There are four items he is entitled to get in respect of each ear, and the same with regard to importers. I think that is what the minister called a blanket arrangement. I will call it an arrangement such as the hon. member for Lake Centre was talking about, under which everybody knows where he stands, and in which the minister exercises his discretion at the outset in framing the regulations, but after that it is the same for everybody. That seems to me to be a sound way to proceed, because then you have, first of all, an over-all arrangement which has many of the qualities for which the hon. member for Lake Centre asked; second you are able to estimate what saving you will make. It seems to me that we are not getting anywhere in this bill until we know roughly what the minister thinks he will save. He has told us what he expects to save in the motor industry. He has told us he has gone into it with the people in industry and he has arrived at arrangements satisfactory to them. That seems to me the wise way to have done it.
In connection with the steel industry, as I recall it, or at any rate in connection with certain of these other items, he said that they had a figure of $100 million in mind, but that it proved not to be enough. What I am

Many of these items can be treated in the same way, and even in those which cannot be treated quite in the same way, I think the illustrations which the minister himself used at Toronto, and which the hon. member for Lake Centre quoted, should enable the minister to give us estimated figures as to the saving which is to be made. I submit that is what we are here for. Suppose, for example, we found that the whole saving to Canada was trivial, would anyone rise in his place in this house, would the minister himself, and say that all these powers were to be given to him for the sake of saving a bagatelle? I have not a copy of that, but I have a few remarks to make on this document because it is relevant to this discussion. Before I make these remarks I should like to say this. As far as the bill is concerned, I am not particularly interested in the details. When the bill was up for second reading I made a statement on it. My opinion was that until this country has control of and develops the basic requirements that will enable it to be an industrial nation, all we shall succeed in doing will be to build assembly plants to assemble our own raw materials that are processed in the United States, and I am not taking back that statement.
I am not going to repeat what the hon. member for Cumberland said a few moments ago, but I agree with it, and I have said it in the house so many times that I am getting tired of hearing myself repeat it. Judging by the document that I hold in my hand, I would say that a large percentage of the capital being invested in new plant and equipment in Canada is accruing from the government in special depreciation allowances to the corporations which are making the new investment. That is my analysis of the document.
With regard to the allocation of expenditures proposed up to March 31, 1949, according to a map that is set out in the document, for the hon. member for Cumberland's information may I say that there is a proposed expenditure of $36,000,000 in British Columbia, $4,000,000 in Alberta, $2,000,000 in Saskatchewan, $2,000,000 in Manitoba, $165 million in Ontario, $159 million in Quebec, $11,000,000 in New Brunswick, $2,000,000 in Nova Scotia, and $1,000,000 in Prince Edward Island. I am not going to say there is any discrimination, but I will say that it is short-sighted investment for this reason. Industry is
Foreign Exchange Conservation

already over-concentrated in the two central provinces. That is clearly indicated by the government's program for the maritimes. I should say they are Ihe displaced provinces of Canada, the depressed areas, and are classified as such by the government. About all that has happened in that end of the country since the end of the war has been to export the people. The Minister of Labour made a statement in the house a few days ago which showed that he seemed to be proud of the fact that they had moved some four thousand people from Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, and that there is still an unemployed population of 4,500 there. If that is the program up to March 31, 1949, it is just a clear indication that not very much will be done to relieve the economic conditions of the maritime provinces. It is time that the people of that end of the country began to realize that the thing to do is to pack up and get out. If we keep on concentrating everything in the two central provinces of Canada what has to be done in the maritimes is for the governments of those provinces to do some government developing of industry themselves and seek overseas markets. They will perhaps have to build a merchant marine themselves to carry their goods across the sea. Unless something along that line is done, the picture is pretty bleak in so far as this particular program is concerned.
I am with the minister in anything he can do to stand Canada on her own feet and remove the domination that exists today in the field of industry and in our whole economy by the United States. My reason for asking the question as to what amount of United States capital was involved in this potential investment was to find out just what the trend is in the direction of further domination from that country.
From reading this document, I gather that the government is making most of the investment in special depreciation allowances, and this means that it is the taxpayers of Canada who are making the investment. If that is so, then, the government should have some say in the allocation of the industry as between one province and another, with the end in view of levelling the economy of this country and seeking new markets elsewhere if it is not economic to transfer our goods from eastern Canada to central Canada.
As the hon. member for Cumberland pointed out a few moments ago, one-third of Canada's basic steel is produced at Sydney, Nova Scotia. It is shipped up to this part of the country, and at rates that keep the plant down there in an uneconomic condition. I think the minister is well aware of that.

Dosco have their fabricating plants in Ontario and Quebec. They sell the raw material to themselves at their own price. They made the government subsidize them during the war. Today they can duck taxes by still continuing to give this material to themselves as cheaply as they want to, because no one exercises any control over them today. If this special depreciation allowance is the major portion of this investment, I think the government should have some say with regard to where these industries are to be established. I personally am becoming ashamed to be talking about conditions in my end of the country. Every time I pick up a government publication with respect to potential development in any part of Canada, the bad end of it is always the end that is really bad at the present time. I think it is nearly time that someone in authority in this country was big enough to get up and lay down a policy for the maritimes, to say that the people are to be moved out or that something will1 be done for them; either one or the other. The people are at least entitled to an honest answer on that question, so that they may not continue to grope around in the dark. I should like the minister to tell me whether I am right or wrong in thinking that the major portion of the investment to be made up to March 31, 1949, is coming out of special1 depreciation allowed- corporations by the government.

-who sits with the C.C.F. group. He says that days of miracles are not past. Well, I hope not. I sincerely trust that the hon. member who made that remark will see a little brighter side so far as the maritimes are concerned and that, as a result of that new outlook, he will help to bring to the maritimes the prosperity which he and others are seeking.
I agree with him in regard to this quick write-off that has been permitted. When firms who invested during the war period are being permitted to write off almost their entire capital expenditure over a period of five years, it strikes the average layman that favouritism is being shown, not in the sense of the minister trying to favour any particular firm but because the large industries were to a great extent concentrated in Ontario and Quebec. Because they enjoyed this large write-off, it naturally gave them equipment at a much lower price than they would otherwise have had to pay, and in that way they have an advantage over those who are trying to develop new industries in other sections of the country. I want the minister to look at this in the broadest possible sense and to give the widest interpretation to his powers as they relate, not to the industrial centres, but to the outlying sections of Canada. For instance, in Halifax at the present time we have a program of construction that centres aro-und steel. Because of the lack of steel and the quota, this program is hampered. The minister might say, "We have given you a quota and we are living up to the quota." I say we should have had granted to the maritime provinces a much larger quota-or, in this case, to Halifax-[DOT] than would apply to other parts of Canada. Instead of the 300 tons a month that were determined on as our quota, the minister might well have said, "Yes, because of the conditions in Nova Scotia, you are entitled to 450,500 or 600 tons in order to bring about greater employment in the shipyards of Halifax."
Then he mentioned stone and referred to the fact that only $400,000 worth of stone was imported. Practically no stone for building purposes should be imported from the United States into Canada. If you go to Nova Scotia and New Brunswick you see stone everywhere. There are two or three stone quarries endeavouring to develop and expand and they find it hard to get the necessary funds from the industrial development bank in order to effect that expansion. I say to the minister who is in charge of this bill that that should be closely linked up with his bill, and it should be made possible to grant these concerns encouragement by helping them in their endeavour to expand. The same thing applies to other projects. Just recently a hew firm, a paint concern, was established in New Glasgow, in Pictou county, with orders waiting to be filled amounting $100,000. I think the minister should encourage that firm by helping them to expand. I refer to Tippets Paint Company which was recently started. I mentioned other firms when I was speaking the other day, and I do not wish to go over them now.
In brief, I am in accord with the remarks made by the hon. member for Cumberland and the hon. member for Cape Breton South in regard to the necessity for greater attention being paid to the maritimes. May I say to the minister, knowing that he is friendly towards our part of the country, that I feel that he would take the broadest interpretation. I used this thought the other day, and I think the same thing could fit into this picture. I said that when applications are made for loans, they should not be treated in the old traditional manner-where the test was: is it a good loan?-but should be dealt with on the basis of the purpose for which the loan is to be used. I say the same thing applies here. When an application for a permit is made from the maritime provinces, particularly from Nova Scotia, I say the guide should not be that the permit is granted on the basis of equality with other parts of Canada but should be on the basis of what good will the granting of that application result in, so far as Nova Scotia is concerned1, in helping out the employment situation.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext:
I have been sitting here patiently, Mr. Chairman, and I thought perhaps I might defer what I am going to say until a later stage. Since the minister said we were free to discuss his opening statement, I want to say one or two things about another matter. Before doing so, however, may I say that I agree completely with what has been said by hon. members from the maritime provinces as to the necessity for distributing industry more widely across Canada. That

Foreign Exchange Conservation
applies not only to the maritime provinces but to western Canada, and particularly to the prairie provinces. The figures read in this house by the hon. member for Cape Breton South emphasize that, instead of concentrating everything in the two central provinces, we should spread it out. I see the hon. member for New Westminster in his place. I well remember a discussion in the war expenditures committee when the establishment of an industry on Vancouver island was suggested because of the iron ore and coal there, and we were told explicitly that there was enough plant in eastern Canada and that, therefore, there was no necesity of developing those resources on Vancouver island. Yet since then, of course, we have had quite a large expansion of that industry in eastern Canada largely, as my hon. friend just pointed out, through accelerated or special depreciation.
I want to say something about the film industry. A few minutes ago the minister said one of the categories we are considering amounted to four or five hundred thousand dollars. Here is an industry to which I think more attention should be paid by the government because, as the minister pointed out in his opening statement this afternoon, it does not involve four or five hundred thousand dollars, but literally millions of dollars that flow from this country, largely to the United States. It is all very well to say that people's habits are pretty well fixed in connection with moving picture theatres. That may be so, but in the last couple of years we have seen that people can enjoy a new type of film. I noticed that the other evening the hon. member for Vancouver East spoke of the Eagle-Lion films that were coming in from Great Britain, made by the Arthur Rank organization, and how enjoyable they were. I do not think we have seen anything in the film industry in recent years to equal " Henry V," produced by that corporation. Some other Odeon films I have seen in which appeared James Mason and others, in my opinion were top-notch and free from much that is objectionable in some of the films we get from the other side of the line.
I believe the government and the country must give some consideration to ways and means of reducing the drain of United' States dollars in this particular field. I have before me a publication issued by the Dominion Bureau of Statistics entitled, "Motion picture theatres, exhibitors and distributors in Canada, 1946." In the general summary it shows that the box-office returns of motion picture theatres in Canada in 1946 amounted to $74,941,966, the highest volume of business on record, and that there was a net increase of 154 theatres over 1945, making the total num-

ber of theatres in Canada 1,477. I may say that at a time when we were short of material for the construction of homes that seems a very large number of theatres to be built in one year. Incidentally, I am told by the Famous Players people in this country that 1946 was a particularly good year and therefore should be taken as the peak; that it was likely to recede rather than increase, and I accept that statement. Of the total box-office returns, the federal and provincial governments collected $15,052,994 in taxes, leaving net receipts of $59,888,972 for the industry, and this amount was eight per cent higher than the net receipts of $55,430,711 recorded in the previous year. This is big business. Paid admissions during the year at the 1,477 theatres numbered 227,538,798, again an increase over the previous year of about six per cent; and incidentally the report says these figures do not include what they call drive-in theatres, for which no figures are available, or itinerant exhibitors, but they do not figure in what I have to say.
The point I am getting at is that fifty per cent of the 1,477 theatres were owned by individuals or firms operating only one theatre, and these houses accounted for only 19-2 per cent of the net receipts and 21-5 per cent of all theatre attendance. Theatres operated by firms owning from four to nineteen theatres comprised 11-7 per cent of the total number and had 11-9 per cent of the total receipts and
12-8 per cent of admissions. Twenty-five per cent of all theatres were operated by firms owning twenty theatres or more, and these obtained 59 per cent of the net receipts and admitted 56-3 per cent of all the persons attending motion picture theatres. The remainder of 13-1 per cent of the theatres were owned by firms owning two or three theatres, and these accounted for 9-5 per cent of total receipts and 9-4 per cent of total admissions.
In his opening statement this afternoon, speaking from memory I believe the minister spoke of some $20,000,000 being spent in film rentals and so on.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext:
No. Just to keep the record
straight, the balance of payments taken out of the country was S20,000,000, of which $17,000,000 was taken out in United States funds and $3,000,000 in sterling.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext:
The balance of payments, including film rentals and so on, was $20,000,000, of which some $17,000,000 was in United States dollars. I think almost every nation faced with the position we are faced with today has had to take some effective steps to meet the situation. We know Great

Foreign Exchange Conservation
Britain has done so. We know France has done so, as well as Norway and Sweden and, most recently, Czechoslovakia. They have endeavoured to find a way of meeting this drain on dollars. I listen to the Canadian actors who perform on the radio on Wednesday evenings, and on "Stage 48" on Sunday evenings, for example. I think the people who produce those programs on the Canadian radio have shown that Canadian dramatic art can reach a very high level. A week ago last evening a Canadian novel "Hetty Dorval" was dramatized. The drama was written by a Canadian associated with the broadcasting corporation; it was played by a group of Canadian actors, and I believe that play would compare with anything I have ever heard over the radio. That shows we can do these things in this country if we will. I do not know whether it is the fault of people who have failed to invest in this kind of thing in Canada that we have no national film organization.
Personally I should like to see a public authority similar to the radio corporation do something in the way of presenting full-length films of Canadian life. I am sure objection would be raised to that immediately. Some might say that could be used as a propaganda weapon. Today the national film board produces a number of excellent shorts and is performing a good service. This afternoon the minister spoke of the wonderful settings available in British Columbia for the making of films, and he referred also to Quebec. Let me say to the committee that other parts of Canada also could provide not only the settings but the stories as well. I know that wonderful stories could be told about the early pioneers in Quebec, and the same could be told of Ontario. The settlement of the prairies, from 1882 on, is an epic story that has never been told and may never be well told. The point is that if it is told, and if a Hollywood film company comes into Canada to do the job on one of our Canadian scenes, it will do it in the Hollywood fashion-one which is not always acceptable.
But, apart from that altogether, except for the hiring of a few extras who may assist in the making of the film in Canada, the whole of the rental of the film will accrue to United States interests. I should like to see something along the lines of what the British are doing, or what some of the other countries are doing. We should endeavour to get a quid pro quo, so that in this country, either through the national film board or, if you like, through the enterprise of Canadian people, we should make a few films dealing with
Canadian life and thereby save the drain on United States dollars. One has only to read this publication by the Dominion Bureau of Statistics and look at the books I have mentioned to realize the truth of what I say. Or, if one really wishes to read the story as it has been written by a man who, incidentally, does not share my political views at all, and who writes purely from the point of view of free enterprise, he should read a book entitled "The First Freedom" by Ernst, which is now available in the parliamentary library. That is a story of the films, press and radio, and a plea for the restoration of private enterprise in those fields. I approve of much of what he says, of course, because he exposes the manner in which great monopolies have been building up in these educational fields. And if one reads this book, as I have read it, particularly the section dealing with the film industry, he will realize that until we make up our minds that we are going to do something to deliver ourselves from the control of the moving picture industry exercised by a single group of people in the United States through their ownership of numerous theatres, and to protect the drain on American dollars, we shall not have accomplished much. In December, after I had made a speech dealing with this particular problem, in which I said: "Why should we prohibit the importation of citrus fruits and neglect this big film field altogether to save United States dollars?" I was informed that the annual exchange cost of the film industry was $10,000,000. not
S17,000,000. The figure I quoted originally was about the same as that quoted by the minister today, or within a very small amount of it.
Certain film interests in Canada wrote and told me I was wrong, and that if I had made all the deductions I should have made it would bring it back to about $10,000,000.

They contend that is all we should count in. But supposing they are right; $10,000,000 is one of the largest categories in these schedules. It is a large drain on our currency. I say that in the exercise of his powers under schedule III the minister should give more thought as to ways and means and should study what has been done in Great Britain, in the Scandinavian countries, in France and Czechoslovakia, with a view to

seeing how we can protect our flow of dollars away from Canada through this particular industry.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: While I am in agreement with much of what the hon. member says, a statement was made a short time ago that most of the British films were controlled by Hollywood capital.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: I cannot say whether or not that is so. But I believe it is true to say that the showing of British films in Canada and in the United States, and of foreign films generally, is controlled by those people who control the bulk of the theatres in the United States and Canada; and they, of course, are Hollywood interests. So that, in reality, perhaps there is some truth in that statement. The minister says we should stop building theatres during this time. I agree with him. According to these figures, 154 were built in 1946, and I think that was too many. But if leniency is to be shown, then I suggest that it should be shown toward any organization which is trying to build theatres to give competition to this tightly owned industry in Canada, and that that should be encouraged. If we are to exercise discrimination, let us exercise it in the right way. The only thing I am doubtful about is as to whether I am correct in this, because I see the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario applauding me when I say that.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: I am applauding the word "competition".

My hon. friend's
applause makes me doubtful as to whether I have said the right thing. However, I have said what I intended to say.
I know that this is an industry in which great interests are involved. I do not want to see Canada play into the hands of any particular interests. This is an industry in which I believe there should be competition, whether that competition is encouraged by the government or is undertaken by private people; because, in the realm of education, competition is, I believe, a very good thing.

speechtext: That is good socialism.

I believe in the right kind of competition. My main criticism against this whole system in Canada is that it is throttling competition and building up great monopolies. It prevents the average man from getting the opportunity to live a full and free life. In a time of depression, what chance has a gifted fellow who must dig ditches or who has to go on relief, to

develop his individuality? Too often we have consigned large numbers of our men to that kind of Telief, where they' are regimented, where there is no opportunity for their personalities to develop or to express themselves properly.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext:
Before returning to the item might I say I found the remarks of the hon. member for Rosetowm-Biggar most interesting. In his words I found a defence of private enterprise when he referred to the development of Canadian industry, and made mention of competition. That was certainly most encouraging; perhaps some of the things we have said are taking effect.
I should like to endorse many of the things the hon. member said about United States films. Perhaps he has not seen the statement made by Sir Henry Wood who said, upon leaving Hollywood, that Hollywood was a national disaster greater than world war II. He said it was a collection of ignorant men [DOT] who ran the industry for the benefit of unhealthy women. I would not go as far as that, but I think we are subjected to a tremendous amount of propaganda which is not altogether healthy as far as Canada is concerned.
I was most interested in the minister's remarks to the hon. member for St. Paul's when he said that, in so far as Bill No. 3 was concerned, the doctrines of the Liberals and the Conservatives differed materially. I do not want to get into an ideological argument with him, but I would suggest that the hon. member's point was well taken. He suggested that the items in schedule III should be either removed to the tariff schedule or dropped altogether as soon as possible, so that business would know whether it was to have protection or whether it would have to compete with imports.
I suggest that there is no need to apologize for a policy which might be called protectionist. As the hon. member for York West has said, this exchange difficulty is chronic. So far as Canada is concerned, we stand it off for a while and then it builds up again. That has been our history for quite a long time. I thing it would be a wise policy on the part of the government in protecting Canadian industry, to let industry know as soon

Foreign Exchange Conservation
as possible whether the items under schedule III are going into the tariff schedule or are to be dropped altogether.
Any industry which might develop under an embargo should be given a chance to prove itself. As the minister is aware, a new project starts off with high costs and high capital expenditures. However, no one can tell what good management or the substitution of certain materials will do in a new business. It is possible and quite probable in many cases that, while a new business will find that they cannot be competitive immediately, they may, through substitution or able management or the use of new processes, be able to reach a competitive position. They might conceivably even become exporters. I strongly urge the minister not to apologize for this policy. We should try to develop every possible industry in the country even if it is necessary to give it protection during its initial period.

A few minutes ago the minister said there was a shortage of steel in every industry in Canada, so, that probably with respect to item 378 and all the other steel and iron items the government is putting no restrictions on their import, but we are prepared to receive every ton of steel and iron that we can get from the United States, and we shall continue to do so in the years to come because we are entirely dependent on steel and iron.

Now that the minister is in charge of the production department, I hope that in some way or another he will bring about the erection of a steel plant in Port Arthur or Fort William, so that that very high grade iron ore-every pound of which is now being shipped out of Canada, with the exception of the very small amount that may go to Sault Ste. Marie for the blast furnace there-may be smelted in one of those cities and rolled into steel of all descriptions, including plate.
Earlier this afternoon an hon. member mentioned the big steel plant at Sydney. It seems to me I have read that, since the war ended, they are not rolling steel as they did while the war was on. That was plate steel, was it not, for ships?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext:
If that is so, it is too bad. If the plate rolling mill at Sydney is closed up or is not operating, it is just too bad for the maritime provinces where they need employment, and where the steel could be turned into ships that will be built because Canada will go along rapidly some time or another. If it ever gets on the way again it will go along rapidly. We have a blast furnace in Montreal; we have none in Toronto. We have two in Hamilton; the Canada Steel Company and the Dominion Foundries and Steel. Some few years ago they started to build a steel mill at Ojibway near Windsor, Ontario. They built two blast furnaces, but they were never used. They are still standing, although they may be obsolete today.
Since there is such a demand for steel in this country, I hope that the minister will use all the influence he can to help build up blast furnaces and steel mills in this country to roll the billets and so forth from Canadian steel. If the time ever comes when the Labrador mines are in operation shipping raw iron, perhaps there will be a great opportunity for a big blast furnace in Quebec. There should be one there. Three Rivers would be an ideal place for a blast furnace. The production mill could be either there or in Montreal. We could then make all these articles which are made from steel.
I understand that H-sections are barred. Is that so?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: No. H-sections come in freely. They are not prohibited.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext:
The item says differently.
Foreign Exchange Conservation

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: That item in the tariff does not include H-sections; it comes under another tariff item.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: At present we make H-sections out of beams and other parts. I do not believe we are rolling H-sections, are we?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: No.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext:
They have to be
imported?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: That is right.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: I notice that last year we imported altogether $762 million worth of 'these products. That is a colossal business. Certainly we ought to be able to save several hundred millions of United States dollars there if we got busy and equipped our own plants to roll the steel that is required. In that way we could use up some of the high grade ore which is now going out of the country. Is it necessary to let it all go out of the country?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: I would not worry about that. On balance we are terrific importers of iron ore; we import ten times as much as we export.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext:
This year I suppose Steep Hock will produce one and a half million tons of ore. Last year they produced one million tons or more. Their objective is three million tons. Three million tons of high grade ore smelted with lower grade ore such as is produced on the Algoma Central railway at Newr Helen mines would mean a large tonnage.
As I have said before, I am looking to the minister to do something in this regard. He is one in the cabinet who has had business experience in a practical way in industry. I do not mean in a legal way; I am talking of things in big industry, in big works. I look to him to do a job for this country. As I said in the session before Christmas, steel is one department in which the minister has a job to do. I am sure I could do a job in it. I will bet any reasonable amount that I could develop in this country a steel industry of considerable magnitude. I know about steel and iron. Since we have the raw ore, it should be second nature to us to roll it and produce all the products that are required. I will help the minister in any way I can to develop a steel industry that we should have in this country. We should cut off entirely at least half of the $762 million worth of steel materials that we now import. We should manufacture $381 million w'orth of it in Canada by Canadian workmen.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext:
We are breaking some new ground here. According to the last answer of the minister, Bill No. 3 was supposed to be a United States dollar saving device. But the very first item that we struck in respect of steel is item 378 which reads:
Bars and rods, of iron -or steel; billets, of iron or steel, weighing less than 65 pounds per lineal yard.
In respect of this item we imported $6,496,000 worth in 1947. There is no saving at all. There will not be any saving this year, next year or, I predict, for a good number of years to come. I think the minister is not taking the committee into his confidence and he is not taking the people into his confidence w'hen he attempts to say to us that, in respect of this steel industry, we are making a saving. I should like to develop that after six o'clock.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: We are considering item 378. Shall the item carry?

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: To continue with item 378, there is one thing the members of the committee now know and it is that there w'ill be no saving of United States dollars on this item or, in fact, on any other steel item in schedule III. It occurs to me that item 378 is either superfluous or is being used for a purpose for which it was never intended. If I understood the minister properly, he says that the item may not be proclaimed. But we should know now, if it is to remain there, what purpose it serves. Through you, Mr. Chairman, I shall recommend to the minister that the item be dropped. If we look at the order in council, P.C. 4678 we find that appendix IX sets down in a blanket way the items which are to be dealt with under this permit system, and now they have all been set out in detail in schedule III. So it is perfectly clear that item 378 was put there with a purpose. I am asking the minister now what this purpose is, why it should remain there, and why it should not be dropped.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS

The reason it is included is that it may be desirable to channel these imports into useful lines. As I stated before, we are short of steel. We are hoping to get more steel. If this item gets larger instead of smaller, that will suit us very well. But

it may be desirable to see that the steel we can get goes to useful 'projects rather than to doubtful ones.

Iron or steel 'angles, beams, channels, columns, girders, joists, tees, zees and other shapes or sections, not punched, drilled or further manufactured than hot rolled, weighing not less than 35 pounds per lineal yard, n.o.p.; piling of iron or steel, not punched or drilled, weighing not less than 35 pounds per lineal yard, including interlocking sections, if any, used therewith, n.o.p.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext:
With respect to items 388, 388a, 388b, 388c and 38Sd, perhaps the minister would not object if they were spoken to in a general way at one time. As I understand it, they represent structural steel, and; structural steel is one of the elements which the minister tells us are to be handled* under the project system. We are short of steel in Canada; we are short of structural steel; and I believe we import most of it from the United1 States. We depend1 upon them for our supply of steel. Bub when an owner or proprietor of a project or company comes to deal with the manufacture or the building of whatever it may be, he is mow compelled to write to the minister setting out the proposition, saying, "We want to go ahead with respect to this project". The minister writes back, in practice as he did in that Toronto board of education case we heard about this afternoon, and he probably says to the applicant, "Have you considered the use of cement or some other commodity"? It may be that the applicant says, "Well, I cannot use cement or I cannot use some other commodity; I must have steel in such and such a quantity". What is to be the final outcome of the matter? Can the applicant proceed with his job, or is he to be stifled? Is the word of the minister with respect to the project to be taken ahead, of that of the applicant. who knows what his economic pursestrings are and who knows how far he can go with the project? If, as a matter of fact, the 'minister is to have the power of life and death over the project, has he or is he to have at his side experts, such as engineers and architects, who will say; "No; steel should not be allowed for this project" or, on the other hand, "Yes, steel should be allowed"? If the minister is to have experts, then of course, it is the case of a clash between the applicant for the material for the project and the engineers who sit at the minister's side. Through you, Mr. Chairman, I should like to ask the minister whether or not there is to be an expert department which is to decide these matters of life and death in the industry.
My next thought on. the matter is this-

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: Down to 388d. Well, he can take 388e too, if he likes. Those are structural steel items. There is no objection to discussing them as a group.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: As long as the committee understands what we are to do it is all right. If it is agreeable to proceed as the hon. member has suggested, we shall do so,

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: I suggested speaking to items 388a, 388b, 388c and 38Sd. I think 388e is in a different category.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: That is right.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: I just wanted to make that clear.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: Then we are dealing with the items down to 388d.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: Yes. I take it that the minister, when he speaks, will say, in so far as these four items are concerned, there will be no saving on steel in 1948, 1949 or 1950. So that, if this project system is to continue, as a matter of fact we are talking about a longterm, long-range policy, and that long-range policy is not to be for just five years or ten years; it may be for twenty years; it may be for the rest of our lifetime, or it may be for the future of Canada. The point I am trying to make with respect to these sections is that, as a matter of fact, there will be no saving this year or in the years to come, or not for a good number of years in the future. The minister will probably say, "Well. I intend to put that steel to work in projects where something will be produced which will be sold in the course of time in the United States and will bring us in United States dollars". I am asking the minister to let us know what those projects are, and what regulations are to govern in respect of those various items. I think I will stop there for the moment.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext:
If a project comes forward that is otherwise a desirable one but 'is using structural steel unnecessarily, the project will be approved, subject to the substitution of a Canadian product for the structural steel. The department has competent engineers who are as well able as anyone else to judge whether that substitution is possible; and if
