the owner is not willing to make the substitution, then, as my hon. friend puts it, he will be stifled.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: Through you, Mr. Chairman, may I ask the minister a direct question? Does the department intend to set up a group of engineers to sit at their elbow and advise on these projects?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: The department has now, and has had for years, a group of engineers; and it will be using them for this particular purpose.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: Are they in the Department of Trade and Commerce?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: No; in the Department of Reconstruction and Supply.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: That brings in another department. This is all under the Department of Trade and Commerce. Does the Minister of Trade and Commerce mean to say that, in order to carry this thing through, he must bring in another department to work out these details? Does he feel that his engineers are more competent to deal with these matters of whether there shall be steel or there shall not be steel than the architect for the party who is putting up the money to build the project?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: This particular program happens to be in the Department of Reconstruction and Supply at the moment. Therefore we use the officers of that department, and in addition we borrow officers from the Department of Trade and Commerce if we need them; both work as one department. We believe our engineers are competent to decide whether concrete can be used instead of structural steel. I have spent most of my life in making such decisions, and I think I am still capable of making them.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: I stated a moment ago, and I should like the minister to tell me if I am wrong, that in respect of his long-range policy, if he is to make it work this thing will be going on for twenty or twenty-five years, and it is possible that neither the minister nor I nor quite a number of us who are here today will be here at that time.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: If neither of us will be here, why worry about it? Let the next generation worry.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: But this is a turning of the road. If I may say so, this is an inverted form of socialism; and if you are not here next year-and I am not suggesting you will not be-we may not have a man who knows all about concrete in charge of these matters.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext:
I thought probably you would
succeed me.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext:
It was a matter of interest and surprise to me to learn, as I understand the minister stated this afternoon, that under these four items there will not actually be any saving in money, because, as a matter of fact, we need all this steel we can get. So that this bill takes on an entirely different complexion. In introducing this measure, and referring to the controls under schedule III, the Minister of Finance said, as reported at page 335 of Hansard for December 16:
This control also involves examination of methods to reduce the net dollar deficiency resulting from many of our industrial operations.
Will the minister tell me whether I am correct in understanding that this has now ceased to be a matter of conserving United States dollars, but that it has now become a means of deciding how this material is to be used? In other words, it is a new control on industry that has nothing whatever to do with saving United States dollars. Is that correct?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: It may be correct, but it has a great deal to do with earning United States dollars. This is the raw material of industry. If it is possible to buy steel at $80 a ton and sell the finished article at $1,000 a ton that is one way to increase exports.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: I am not denying that statement, but it seems to me that this gives a very curious, unexpected and unintended, as far as I was concerned, use to this act.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: Very logical, though, is it not?

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: Does the minister now suggest that the scope of this act is not merely to say, "We will cut down purchases from the United States," but that in addition you may say, "We will bring in certain things from the United States which will not result in any saving, but by our wisdom we will so direct them that they will contribute more United States dollars"? Is that what the minister is saying?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: Quite.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: At the moment I do not say whether that is good or bad in itself. It may be good, but it is certainly an unexpected result under this act.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext:
Well, I am sorry to surprise my hon. friend.

Foreign Exchange Conservation

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: Perhaps I am not the only one to be surprised.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: Referring to what the minister had to say this afternoon with respect to new industries, I am interested in having the minister develop that point for a moment. He suggested that new industries coming along which might want some of this steel would have more or less to prove themselves to him or his department ; in other words, that they would have to show they would be able to compete with other industry in the country. I take it that is simply making a monopoly of the industries already in existence. I would ask the minister to explain if that is not so, if we are not creating monopolies under this bill instead of helping the industry of the country?

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: What monopoly is my hon. friend suggesting we are creating? Name one.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: I am only following up what the minister had to say. I understood him to say that if a new industry wants to commence operation; if it wants to build a mill to carry on a new project, he will have to know that it will be able to compete with other companies in the same line of business; otherwise it will not be able to start. What is that but a monopoly?

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: Would the minister say whether he expects to be able to follow this program through with the present staff of trade and commerce and reconstruction and supply, or will he need' additional staff?

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: It is not anticipated that any great additional staff will be needed. We may need the odd man; but, as at present contemplated, it is not thought there will be any substantial increase in the combined staffs.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: I am informed that a good deal of this material, particularly under item 388b, is ordinarily dealt with through distributors in the industry. Will the minister say if that is correct?

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: That is correct.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: So that, particularly under item 388b, the stuff would come in and would be handled by a distributor, from whom it would be obtained by the ordinary consumers, many of them small people such as blacksmith establishments in small towns and that sort of thing, I presume? Will the minister say whether that is correct?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: Then will the minister explain how the permits will be worked? Is there to be a permit to the distributor, and will he then allocate it to the trade; or has he to satisfy some government authority as to the propriety of every small bit of material he furnishes to the trade?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: The process is just being worked- out. It is pro-bable that the distributors will receive blanket permits, and will be required to account for the steel they import. If some of their steel turns up in a project which has not been authorized it will be just too bad for the distributor.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: As I understand the minister, right now all these twenty-eight fabricators of steel in Canada, if that is the number, are getting their steel and ore from the United States without a permit?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: But as I understand it, and the minister will correct me if I am wrong, when they come to deliver that steel, or to accept orders for it, those orders will have to be screened by the minister or his department, so that he will say, "You may send that steel to this project," or "You may not send it." Am I right in that?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: That is right.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: So, as a matter of fact, these four items do not mean a thing at the present time as far as the importation of steel from the United States is concerned? The steel is coming in anyway, whether or not these sections are here?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: But may I point out to my hon. friend that I have no legislation at the moment which allows me to interfere with it. When you get through debating this bill, perhaps I can start.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: That is not being fair, if I may say so.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: Of course it is.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext:
The minister has had
power since November 18, under order in council 4678. He cannot deny that appendix IX gives him all the power he needs. The only thing is that all these things are not enumerated. I am putting it to the minister that he is in an awful hurry to do something which may take, ten, twenty or thirty years to carry through. As a matter of fact, he should not be in a hurry at all about this matter. This has to do with the whole future of this country; and he should be telling the committee as he reluctantly told us with respect to the automobile industry, what the regulations will be and how it will be worked out.

Foreign Exchange Conservation
With respect to the steel industry, which is probably the most important factor in the whole bill, so far as the building of Canadian industry within our own country is concerned, I suggest that the minister should tell us at this time upon what formula we are to work, so that we may know, so that the public may know and so that industry may know. speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: I will bring forward formulae. I have brought forward formulae for the automobile industry and, if my hon. friend will get on a bit with this thing, I will bring in other formulae. subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext:
Evidently, from the
minister's speeches, this is something which will be handled with the co-ordination of industry. I believe that is the expression he has used. I suggest there is no rush about this matter, so far as steel is concerned. We are not going to save any money for-

speechtext: We are not rushing, are we? I would not worry about that. We have been three months on it now.

speechtext: I suggest to the minister that he ought not to be rushing us in respect of these items until he has formulated some sort of regulations or policy. subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS

speechtext: I do not think that helps the debate any. I am sure I do not take any slaps at anybody else. I have travelled on United States highways. I took a trip to Vancouver last fall, a distance of about 1,200 miles from my home, and, after obtaining a report respecting some of the roads on the all-Canada route, I decided I would not take a chance on that route, and went by United States roads. Arriving at Vancouver, I stayed at a small auto-court and, while there, met one or two United States tourists. Seeing my Alberta licence, they asked me if I had come over such-and-such a highway. I said, "No, I did not; I came over an American route." "Well," they said, "good for you; we came over that highway, but, believe me, we will never go back on it." That is the sort of thing one hears said. The tourist trade means a lot in connection with this exchange program. When tourists ride over tfed roads they gain certain impressions. They do not say, "Oh, well, I suppose we will have to stand it; Canada is in dire need of American dollars to buy our machinery." They . do not say that. Rather, they say, "Well, if that is the kind of stuff we get when we come to Canada, never again." The result is that, even if we do repair our roads, they have memories.
We have some wonderful tourist attractions in Canada. I am not pitting the east against the west, because this eastern country is very beautiful indeed. But the mountainous regions of Alberta and British Columbia cannot be surpassed anywhere. This is the time when United States tourists are going to take trips, and whether they take them in Canada will depend upon the conditions of our highways.

speechtext: May I ask the minister why there is this distinction between the items in schedules I and II whereby we work under a strict formula as to how much we shall allow in from the United States and how much we shall allow in from the United Kingdom and the items in schedule III where we have no formula worked out? Yes. That will enable the committee more easily to see the results of the amendments which will be moved.
I have stated on previous occasions in connection with this tax program that I hope to be

Excise Tax Act Amendment
able to adapt it to the changing needs and circumstances of a situation to which I have been devoting the closest study, and to introduce relaxations or modifications from time to time where I felt that changes could be made without doing injury to our main purpose. I must say that in several cases, after discussing the matter fully with the representatives of an industry, and an exchange of views of mutual benefit, I have decided that, on balance, the tax should not be imposed.
An instance of the sort of consideration which has moved me to amend the application of the tax has been where there already exists an export flow of Canadian goods to the United States or where manufacturers have given assurance of such an export and this export of goods was jeopardized by the imposition of the excise tax. Such a situation can arise because of a procedure followed by the United States customs authorities in determining the dutiable value of an import into the United States for purposes of their tariff.
Under this procedure the amount of such a tax as our 25 per cent excise tax is added to the value otherwise subject to duty, with a consequent increase in the total duty payable. On balance, as a result of this procedure in several instances we stood to suffer a loss of exports to the United States, and it is for this reason that I am proposing that the tax be not imposed in the case, for example, of sporting goods, oil burners and oil burning equipment, hot plates and grills.
Another group of changes have the effect of limiting the tax to the household use of the articles concerned, where it was felt that the tax should not be applied to certain classes of capital equipment. Accordingly, the tax will have this more limited application in the case of food or drink mixers, food choppers or grinders, irons and ironers, vacuum cleaners, floor waxers and polishers.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Washing machines?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
No, they are not in general industrial use, and never were. I am saying that the tax is being relaxed. We are limiting the tax, generally speaking, to the household use of the articles concerned; and1 where they are in the nature of capital goods, used in industrial enterprise, as part of the cost of production, the tax is not being imposed.
In other cases which were gone into carefully it was established to my satisfaction that undue hardship either to consumers or producers would have resulted from the tax, and for this reason I have decided not to ask the committee to impose a tax in these cases. It
was because of consideration of this sort that I have withdrawn my recommendation for a tax on musical instruments.
From the resolutions as amended, the committee will see that, although I have been willing to adjust the tax program where it seemed reasonable to do so, the main body of the program as I announced it on November 17 remains substantially intact. The tax will cover the important range of items such as automobiles, motor cycles, radios and phonographs, refrigerators, vacuum cleaners, outboard motors, firearms, miscellaneous electrical appliances, projectors, cameras and films and some toilet articles.
Just to have it in the proper form, I will ask one of my colleagues to move the amendment which will put into effect the changes which have been decided upon since I moved the resolution on December 19.

For more than 700 years, since the time of King John and the Magna Carta, it has been a recognized principle in all British nations that only parliament can impose taxation on the people. One of the kings of England lost his head because he tried to deviate from that principle. It would seem that the Minister of Finance does not consider it necessary to follow the lessons of history. It means that executive government, as represented by the minister, by his officials, by his assistants, most of whom are not members of parliament, has imposed a tax on Canadians arbitrarily and autocratic-

ally. The minister is only asking parliament for approval two months after the tax went into effect.
I suggest that if this resolution goes through, perhaps a few years from now, the government will decide that it can put through taxes without even bothering to come to parliament for approval. Surely that is conceivable. If this resolution is passed, we shall have created a precedent, which will 'mean that, in the future, the government will be able to impose taxes and then, three months or six months' afterwards, come to parliament and say, "We have imposed these taxes; approve them." I think even members on the government side will object to that usurping of parliament's authority. I ask the hon. member for Comox-Alberni what he thinks of it.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: I do object.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: The hon. member has voted many times against the government. I hope he will make a statement as to whether he likes this usurping of parliament's powers.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: I have not the eloquence of my hon. friend or I would.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: W'hat has the minister to say about this taxation by order in council?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: No order in council.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I should like to quote what he said, as reported on page 359 of Hansard of December 16, 1947:
I say I am not claiming the right to tax the Canadian people. It is nothing more than a notice that the tax will be imposed if parliament approves.
I wonder if the minister is trying to kid someone.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: It is done every year when the budget is presented.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Notice his statement:
It is nothing more than a notice that the tax will be imposed if parliament approves,
I say that statement of the minister is not a correct one.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Absolutely correct.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Parliament at this
moment has not approved; yet these taxes have been collected for more than two months. Anyone who tries to purchase a washing machine or a refrigerator or one of the items affected will soon find out whether the amount of money involved is a "notice" or whether it is a "tax". Ask any housewife. The minister in his speech just claimed that the levy was

Excise Tax Act Amendment
only a "notice". However, a little later on, he decided that, after all, it might be a tax, because he said:
I shall ask parliament to make this tax retroactive.
The minister then proceeded to argue that the notice was a tax, but that, after all, there is nothing wrong with taxing by notice.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: No order in council.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
The minister says the tax was imposed as is dona when the budget resolutions are tabled. May I suggest that the way in whicn this excise tax was imposed is eompletly different from the way in which budget resolutions are brought down. When budget resolutions are involved the taxing authorities are notified the night the budget is brought down that the resolutions are before parliament and that the officials are to start collecting the tax. In the present case, the taxing officials were notified that the tax would be brought before parliament in the future, but they were instructed to collect the tax immediately. I ask the committee to note the difference. In the case of the budget, "the taxes are before parliament"; in the case of the excise tax, "the taxes will be brought before parliament", perhaps a month, perhaps three months, or perhaps a year from now. In the meantime collect the tax-those were the instructions given to the tax officials.
I suggest that the issue involved in the resolution before us tonight is clearcut:	Are
Canadians to be taxed by arbitrary order in council, or are they to be taxed by their democratically elected parliament? That is the issue, and I challenge any member of this house to say that is not the issue. I know that many members on the government side of the house were more surprised than members of the opposition when the minister brought down this excise tax. If they are still angry, let me suggest that the way to register their anger is by voting against this resolution.
What about the tax itself? In the first place, I would suggest that if ever there was an inflationary tax brought before this parliament, this is one. When parliament was called into emergency session less than three months ago, the members were told by the government that one of the main reasons for calling this emergency session was to cope with the problem of the rising cost of living. We were here only a few weeks when the price spreads committee was set up, to investigate why prices were going up and how we might bring them down. The committee was
given fairly wide powers, and it is today calling witnesses from all over Canada. I would suggest to the chairman of that committee, the Minister of National Health and Welfare, if he were here, that he is overlooking the star witness, the man who has contributed more than anyone else to high prices in Canada-the Minister of Finance.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Off with his head.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
For a year or two I have listened to the Minister of Finance telling Canadian businesses that they must keep prices down. He preaches one thing, but in actual practice he does precisely the opposite. He adopts a policy which forces prices up. I challenge the price spreads committee to subpoena the Minister of Finance. Let him try to justify before that committee the recent price increases in washing machines, refrigerators and other electric appliances. Let him explain the adverse effect which this tax is having on the cost of living. In taxing these necessities of life 25 per cent, the minister is adding to the cost of living and pushing the spiral of inflation that much further upward.
In addition to being inflationary, this is a vicious tax. It is an indirect levy which bears most heavily on the little man who can least afford to bear it. It hits him at a time when he is finding it ever more difficult to meet the rising cost of living. This tax hits the veteran who is trying to start up a home. It hits young married couples who are starting up housekeeping. It hits the small taxpayer.
What reason does the minister give us for this tax? Look at the explanation given by the minister at page 336 of Hansard, where he said:
Tire first and primary purpose is to discourage the sort of expenditure which adds to our imports from the United States.
In other words, if I understand the matter correctly, many of these articles, refrigerators, cars, washing machines, and so forth, which are made in Canada, use a certain number of United States parts. I can understand the necessity of keeping these expenditures at a minimum. But surely it would have been more equitable to put these articles and parts on a quota basis, instead of imposing on Canadians this excise tax.
The minister went on to say:
Without these taxes, prices of many of the articles affected could have risen a good deal, to the benefit of the manufacturers and distributors.
Excise Tax Act Amendment

The minister knows very well that this would not have been so, if price controls had been reimposed on these articles. I submit to the committee that if these articles had been put on a quota basis in the bill we have just been discussing just as much or more United States exchange would have been saved as by imposing this excise tax.
What was the minister's second reason for this tax? I quote from page 336 of Hansard again:
... to limit so far as practicable the degree of discrimination against regular suppliers in the United States and their dealer organizations in Canada.
What kind of reason is that? Is it a reason dictated by some bureau in Washington? Apparently the minister and the government are willing to discriminate against the small Canadian taxpayer, against the veteran, against the housewife, but they will not discriminate against United States business firms.
I quote again from the minister's statement:
By imposing these excise taxes, we aTe doing something to protect the legitimate longer-range interests of these businesses.
In effect, the minister says: Discrimination against Canadians is regrettable but it is all right; but under no circumstances shall we discriminate against United1 States business firms. I submit that the minister's second reason for this excise tax is not a good one.
But his third reason is even weaker than the other two. His third reason is the need for more revenue. He says, at page 336 of Hansard:
. .	. additional revenue will not be unwelcome. . .
. . . our budget position, though good, is not as good as many popular reports would have it.
It has been estimated that the government will have a surplus this year of approximately three-quarters of a billion dollars. If I am correct the government is taking over a billion dollars, or almost 40 per cent of the total taxation, in indirect taxes, and now it proposes further to increase the load on the people of small means who can ill afford to pay. At a time when the government is showing such a huge surplus, a surplus which, I believe, is greater than- ad the other surpluses put together since confederation, surely it cannot say that it needs more revenue. That cannot be used as an excuse for this kind of tax.
I dislike exaggerated statements and I try not to make them. I hope I am not making [DOT]one now when I say that, in my opinion, if the government imposes this tax it can be accused, in view of its huge surplus, of being guilty of legalized robbery of the taxpayers

of Canada. This party will1 do all in its power to defeat the resolution. We shall vote against it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I should like to deal with one or two points just raised by the hon. member for Moose Jaw. First, as to the illegality of the 'tax, I made it perfectly clear in my radio address, and again in the house, that in announcing the imposition of this tax the government was giving notice to the people of Canada who would be affected by it that parliament would be asked to impose this tax and impose it retroactively to the night I made my announcement.
As the committee knows, the usual budgetary practice is for the Minister of Finance to bring in his budget resolutions and make his budget speech when the house is sitting. The resolutions are tabled and notice is given rhat the taxes will be effective as from that day, although in fact they may not be approved by parliament for six weeks or more.
It is quite true that I made my announcement on November 17 when parliament was not sitting, but I stated in my radio broadcast on November 17 that parliament had already been called into emergency session for December 6 and that these resolutions would be brought before parliament as soon as it convened. And they were. So that in fact the notice which is ordinarily given under budgetary practice in this house was given two weeks ahead for obvious reasons. If this tax were to be part of the government's emergency exchange conservation program and were to be announced at the same time as the other measures, it is quite clear that notice had to be given that parliament would be asked to make the tax effective as from that day. It is quite clear that it had to be; that notice had to be given that the resolutions would be made effective; that parliament would be asked to make them effective as from that date, or individual persons could have derived a great deal of advantage from them.
The committee may criticize that procedure; they may say that it is improper, if they will. I do not think it was in the circumstances; but in essence, it is exactly the same procedure as is followed when the budget is brought down, save that we anticipated the calling of parliament by some ten days or two weeks.
Now, with regard to the excise taxes being inflationary, I do not agree that they are inflationary. I think that they are just the reverse; that they are deflationary, if anything. One of the means of combatting inflation, when there is an excess of purchasing power,

Excise Tax Act Amendment
is by imposing taxes such as these that drain off purchasing power. Far from their being inflationary, they will have, if anything, a deflationary effect.
Does not every increase in price do the same thing?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Precisely. Every increase in price does the same thing.
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That is all right. All the experts on inflation seem to be sitting in this house. The particular articles that are included in this list are not, in their essence, necessities of life. In the great majority of cases they are articles, the purchase of which the people can defer for a time. On the other hand, df they wish to spend their money on a motorcar, a motorcycle, or a new refrigerator, then they have that much less money to spend on other goods which are in short supply and thereby drive up the prices. I do not wish or desire to get into an argument tonight on whether the taxes are inflationary or not. I make the assertion here that they are not inflationary. My hon. friend says they are.
It is true that references have been made to increases in taxes, but in the discussion of this matter I have not heard a single hon. member on any side of the house refer to the taxes which were removed at the same time that these taxes were announced. I refer to the sales tax on domestic sales of electricity, which affects practically everyone in this country who uses it, and the removal of one cent a pound tax on sugar, which affects pretty nearly everybody in this country. Nobody has made any reference to these. In my broadcast speech I mentioned that these taxes were being taken off some of the necessities ol life; I emphasized that the primary purpose of this special emergency tax was not for revenue, and I demonstrated that in part at any rate, by removing these other taxes. Hon. members who pay electric light bills-and I suppose most of them do-have already noticed the tax reduction on their bills, and that is something which will go on for month after month and year after year. These emergency excise taxes are admittedly temporary taxes. As I say, I do not want to make a long speech tonight, but I did want to answer these two points which were raised by the hon. member for Moose Jaw.

It was our thought when, perhaps by an excess of the Christmas spirit, we allowed ourselves to go into committee just before Christmas, that the proper course to follow was to
deal with the details of the bill and we were
not going to make any speeches until second reading. Since the matter has been brought up, I should like, even in the few minutes that are left, to deal with one point which has been made by the hon. member for Moose Jaw. May I preface that by saying I am astounded more than I can say to hear the Minister of Finance say that there is really no difference between the situation which arises when the budget speech is made, the effect of which we all know, on the one hand, and what was done last November 17 when the minister did not, as he said, pass an order in council, but said that a request would be made. I am maintaining that there is all the difference in the world, a practical difference, in the two. When the Minister of Finance rises in his place in this house and reads his budget speech, it is quite true that the resolutions are put forward and then they become law in the form of bills in perhaps some weeks or months. But from that very moment it is competent for hon. members to say. We will have none of it. It is competent for parliament to say that. It does not very often happen because, after all, the government has its majority; it brings in these bills, and of course they go through in practically every case.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If they did not the government would be defeated.

I maintain there is a whole world of difference. When they come before parliament it is competent for the elected representatives of the people then and there to say, We will not have it. If they do not do that, by acquiescence they really support them.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: They cannot do it without a vote.

On the other hand, what do we have here? We have a minister three weeks before parliament is assembled, and it might have been, on the same line of reasoning, three months or six months, making the announcement over the air. To suggest in any way that this is comparable with what takes place when the budget is announced is to compare two things that are entirely unreal. The practical difference is also very great. I agree with what the hon. member for Moose Jaw said. It is quite true perhaps he made a verbal slip with regard to the order in council; but I felt badly that there should be ministers of the crown sitting in this house and regarding this apparently as a joke. It is a tremendously serious thing, and it seems to me that it
Excise Tax Act Amendment

should be so regarded. There should be no doubt whatever that what was done last November was a most improper thing, and incidentally there was no reason for it. The minister has told us that they were considering this months ahead. There was any amount of time to have summoned parliament and to have done the thing in the proper way which has the sanction of centuries behind it.
As the hon. member for Moose Jaw said, this precedent can be used by governments that might be even much worse than this government-
That is not possible.
-and have philosophies that this government would greatly reprobate, just as I would reprobate them. Unfortunately this is a predent which has been set, Mr. Chairman. May I call it eleven o'clock?

Before the committee rises, I should like to ask the Minister of Finance one question. A moment ago he was dealing with the propriety of collecting if not imposing taxes, as was done on November 17, by decree, by address, by a speech over the air, as compared with doing it when the budget is brought down. He was defending the action he had taken. The question I want to ask is this. Can he tell the committee of any single instance in the history of Canada or in the history of Britain, where a tax has been imposed and collected in this way by an address of the minister when the house was not in session?
Charles I.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not know about the history of Britain. So far as I know, there has never been a case in Canada where notice of the proposed imposition of taxes has been given prior to the calling of parliament, when parliament was not in session, and notice given at the same time that it would be made retroactive, that parliament would be asked to make it retroactive.
Bennett did it in the sugar tax and they all profited by it.

That is a good precedent.
Progress reported.
May I ask the minister what the business will be tomorrow?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We shall take first second reading of the farm improvement loan measure which was given first reading today. No, perhaps, first, we might take third reading of Bill No. 3, which was given second reading today; then, second, when that is concluded, second reading of the farm loan improvement measure; after that, continuation of discussion in committee on the tax resolution which we have been considering this evening. Assuming they are finished, we then might proceed with second reading of Bill No. 7, which is the gold measure.

At eleven o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
